summary: Describes a way to have an arbitrary number of Rendezvous Points per group in a single PIM Sparse Mode domain by combining PIM and the Multicast Source Discovery Protocol. This gives load sharing and redundancy for multicast rendezvous.

plainLanguage.summary: Anycast RP lets several routers act as rendezvous points for the same multicast group while sharing one anycast address. MSDP keeps the routers informed about active sources.

questions: why does anycast rp need msdp
what is a rendezvous point in pim
how does anycast rp fail over
subtitle: A way for several PIM-SM routers to share one rendezvous-point address using MSDP.

tldr.problem: PIM-SM traditionally uses one active rendezvous point per group, which can concentrate traffic and make sources depend on a distant router.
tldr.mechanism: Several rendezvous points use the same anycast address so senders reach a topologically close point. They use unique unicast addresses to peer over MSDP and share source information.
tldr.outcome: The method supports multiple active rendezvous points and faster fail-over, but MSDP use creates (S,G) state along the receiver-to-source path.

today: RFC 3446 is an Informational memo from January 2003, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes a mechanism using PIM and MSDP.

sections.title: What Anycast RP Provides
sections.content:
PIM Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) allows only one active rendezvous point (RP) per group. Anycast RP allows an arbitrary number of RPs per group in one PIM-SM domain.

The memo aims to improve fail-over time and share register-decapsulation load. MSDP is required so the RPs maintain a consistent view of active sources; a domain using Anycast RP does not have to run MBGP.
sections.plainLanguage: Anycast RP lets multiple routers serve the same multicast group. They use MSDP to share information about which sources are active.

sections.title: Limits of a Single Rendezvous Point
sections.content:
With one active RP, traffic can concentrate at that router. Splitting the multicast group range among RPs can distribute load, but operators may not know traffic levels in advance and periodic reconfiguration scales poorly.

Receivers and sources may also send joins toward an RP far away from their region. The memo notes this can cause data to cross an expensive link twice and leave local users dependent on a distant RP.
sections.plainLanguage: One RP can concentrate work and sit far from sources or receivers. Anycast RP lets routing direct each sender toward a nearby RP instead.

sections.title: Configuring an Anycast RP Set
sections.content:
Every RP in a set serving a group uses the same anycast address and advertises consistent group-to-RP mappings. Senders then register toward the topologically closest RP. Each RP uses its own unique unicast address for its MSDP peerings.

All routers in the domain must be able to reach the anycast address. The memo says the address must not be used as an RP's router ID or as the RP address in Source Active messages, because those uses can prevent peerings or make the peer-RPF check fail.
sections.plainLanguage: Give each RP the same anycast address but a unique unicast address for MSDP peering. Configure the same group mappings and make the anycast address reachable throughout the domain.

sections.title: MSDP Peer Checks and State
sections.content:
MSDP peers forward Source Active messages away from the originating RP using a peer reverse-path-forwarding check. The check uses routing information to identify the peer that is the next hop toward that RP.

The anycast address must not appear as the RP address in those messages. The memo also notes that using MSDP this way creates (S,G) state along the path from receiver to source; that state may not exist when receivers stay on a shared tree with a single RP.
sections.plainLanguage: MSDP peers use the originating RP's address to check where Source Active messages came from. The anycast address cannot replace that unique origin address.

sections.title: Protecting Routing and Peer Messages
sections.content:
The design relies on anycast addressing, so the memo warns operators to guard against spoofing and protect unicast routing and the PIM RPs.

It describes keyed MD5 or IPsec as ways to protect unicast routing, recommends PIM message-integrity and origin-authentication mechanisms, and notes that MSDP peers can use keyed MD5. Unstable unicast routing can also make RP selection unstable.
sections.plainLanguage: Protect routing, PIM, and MSDP communications against spoofing and modification. If unicast routing changes unpredictably, the RP selected by a source or receiver can change too.
